title: ShopFloor AI
summary_easy: ShopFloor AI predicts milling machine failures from five sensor readings, streams sensor KPIs and alerts through Kafka, and answers maintenance questions with a RAG assistant, all as one Docker Compose stack with MLflow and Airflow. On the synthetic AI4I 2020 dataset its gradient boosting model reached 0.85 F1 and 0.96 AUC. Reading the code back shows several connections between the parts that do not yet work as described, which Tanay owns as the main lesson.
summary_deep: The AI4I 2020 dataset (10,000 synthetic runs, 3.39% failures, five rule generated failure modes) feeds 16 model inputs: five raw sensors, an encoded product grade, and ten derived features such as power (torque times angular speed), temperature gap, and wear times torque, which mirror the dataset's own failure rules. Three scikit-learn pipelines are trained on a stratified 80/20 split and logged to MLflow; gradient boosting (200 trees, depth 6, subsample 0.8) reached 0.8548 F1 and 0.9591 AUC, random forest 0.8387 and 0.9823, logistic regression 0.3054 and 0.9455, and the best by F1 is registered. FastAPI loads the latest registered version and a LangChain RetrievalQA chain (800 character chunks, text-embedding-3-small, ChromaDB, MMR top 4 of 8, gpt-4o-mini). A Kafka producer replays rows and a consumer keeps a 100 record window with threshold alerts and cooldowns. Airflow retrains nightly behind a 0.80 F1 branch. Caveats Tanay states plainly: the data is synthetic, the threshold is the untuned 0.5, training registers before the gate so the gate does not protect serving, the serving path encodes every grade the same, the stream never calls the model, and RAG refreshes duplicate chunks.

sheet.easy:
## ShopFloor AI in one line
Predict machine failures from sensor readings, stream KPIs and alerts through Kafka, and answer maintenance questions with RAG, as one Docker Compose stack.

## The data
AI4I 2020 (UCI, CC BY 4.0): 10,000 synthetic milling runs, 3.39% failures, five failure modes (tool wear, heat dissipation, power, overstrain, random), product grades L 50%, M 30%, H 20%.

## Results (one stratified 80/20 split, synthetic data)
| Model | F1 | AUC-ROC |
|---|---|---|
| Gradient Boosting (selected) | 0.8548 | 0.9591 |
| Random Forest | 0.8387 | 0.9823 |
| Logistic Regression | 0.3054 | 0.9455 |

## The pieces
- 16 model inputs: 5 raw sensors plus 11 engineered (power, temperature gap, wear times torque, flags).
- MLflow tracks 3 models per run and registers the best by F1.
- FastAPI /predict, /ask, /health; Streamlit with 4 pages.
- Kafka producer replays rows; consumer keeps a 100 row window and alerts.
- RAG: 6 SOPs, 800 character chunks, OpenAI embeddings, ChromaDB, MMR top 4, gpt-4o-mini.
- Airflow nightly at 2 AM: check data, train, gate at 0.80 F1, refresh RAG.

## Say this out loud
- The data is synthetic and the features mirror the rules that generated the labels.
- Random Forest had the better AUC; I chose on F1 at the default threshold.
- The 0.80 gate does not block registration as written; the API serves the latest version.

## Gaps worth owning
Gate registers before checking, serving encodes every grade the same, stream never calls the model, Airflow containers miss config, RAG refresh duplicates chunks, CI file not in the repo, drift page is a rolling mean.

## Architecture
```
Streamlit (8501) --HTTP--> FastAPI (8001): /predict /ask /rag/ingest /health
  lifespan: mlflow.sklearn.load_model("models:/failure-predictor/latest"); RAG chain
  MLflow 2.16.0 (5000): sqlite backend, artifacts ./data/models
  ChromaDB 0.5.0 (8000): collection milling_sops
Kafka 7.6.0 + Zookeeper: shopfloor.sensor.raw -> consumer (window 100) -> shopfloor.alerts
  listeners: kafka:29092 (containers), localhost:9092 (host)
Airflow 2.9.3 shopfloor_retrain, 0 2 * * *: check_data >> train >> should_register >> [register | skip] >> refresh_rag
```
Compose entries: zookeeper, kafka, mlflow, chromadb, airflow-init, airflow-webserver, airflow-scheduler, api, dashboard (9; 7 with Airflow counted once). Producer and consumer run on the host.

## Data (UCI AI4I 2020)
10,000 rows; Type L 50%, M 30%, H 20%; air T random walk std 2 K around 300 K; process T = air + 10 K with std 1 K; rpm from 2860 W with noise; torque N(40, 10) Nm; wear +5/+3/+2 min for H/M/L.
| Mode | Rule | Count (hard coded in download.py) |
|---|---|---|
| TWF | wear time drawn in 200 to 240 min | 46 |
| HDF | $\Delta T < 8.6$ K and rpm < 1380 | 115 |
| PWF | P < 3500 W or P > 9000 W | 95 |
| OSF | wear x torque > 11,000 / 12,000 / 13,000 minNm (L/M/H) | 98 |
| RNF | 0.1% random | 5 |
Machine failure = any mode; 339 total (3.39%).

## Features (16 inputs)
Raw 5; type_encoded; $\Delta T$; $P = \tau \cdot 2\pi n/60$; wear x torque; wear/240; torque/(rpm+1); P<3500; P>9000; hdf_risk ($\Delta T$<10 and rpm<1500); (air-300)/2; (process-310)/1.

## Models (train.py)
Split 80/20, stratified, random_state 42 (test about 2,000 rows, about 68 failures by arithmetic).
| Model | Config | F1 | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|
| GradientBoosting | 200 trees, depth 6, lr 0.1, subsample 0.8 | 0.8548 | 0.9591 |
| RandomForest | 200 trees, depth 12, min split 5, balanced | 0.8387 | 0.9823 |
| LogisticRegression | scaler, max_iter 1000, balanced | 0.3054 | 0.9455 |
Logged: accuracy, precision, recall, f1, roc_auc, cv_f1_mean, cv_f1_std (5 fold), params, model with input example, importances, report. Selection: max F1; register via search_runs ordered by F1.

## Formulas
$$F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P+R},\quad \mathrm{AUC} = \Pr(s(x^+) > s(x^-))$$
$$F_M(x) = F_0(x) + \sum_m \nu h_m(x),\ \ r_i = y_i - p_i$$
$$w_c = \frac{n}{k\,n_c}\ \ (\text{failure} \approx 14.7,\ \text{pass} \approx 0.52)$$
$$t^* = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP}+c_{FN}}$$
$$\mathrm{MMR} = \arg\max_{d \in C\setminus S}\left[\lambda\,\mathrm{sim}(d,q) - (1-\lambda)\max_{d' \in S}\mathrm{sim}(d,d')\right]$$

## Serving
/predict: engineer_features on one row, predict_proba, threshold 0.5, risk factors (wear > 200, P outside 3500 to 9000, $\Delta T$ < 8.6 and rpm < 1380, torque > 55). Bug: LabelEncoder refit on one row maps every Type to 0 (H at training).

## Registry and gate
register_model creates a new version; API loads latest at startup; no alias or stage. DAG: train registers (register_best=True) before should_register; register task only prints. Stages are deprecated in MLflow in favor of aliases.

## Streaming
Producer: JSON, key = Type, acks all, flush every 50, 0.5 s interval (10,000 rows about 83 min by arithmetic). Consumer: group shopfloor-consumer, offset reset latest, deque(100), rolling failure rate from ground truth labels, torque average, temp gap average; alerts > 5% failure (CRITICAL), torque > 60 (WARNING), wear > 200 (WARNING), 60 s cooldown per type. No model call.

## RAG
6 hand written SOPs; RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter 800 / 100; text-embedding-3-small; Chroma HttpClient; MMR k 4, fetch_k 8; RetrievalQA stuff; gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0.1, max_tokens 1024; prompt asks for citations and refusal when absent. Re ingest appends duplicates. No evaluation.

## Tests (15)
Data 5, features 4, streaming 4, SOPs 2. Untested: train, gate, API, registry, RAG answers, DAG.

## Mismatches found
MLflow 5000 in compose vs 5001 in docs; CI workflow and .env.example referenced but absent; README value range check absent in DAG; Airflow containers lack configs, MLflow URI, shared DB.

| Number | Source |

| 10,000 rows, 3.39% failures | portfolio, UCI |
| 16 features, 3 models, 7 services, 6 SOPs, 15 tests | portfolio, README |
| 0.80 F1 gate | portfolio, retrain_dag.py |
| window 100, alert 5% / 60 Nm / 200 min, cooldown 60 s | consumer.py |
| chunk 800 / 100, k 4, fetch_k 8 | rag/engine.py |

narration.script: The problem is unplanned machine failures on a milling line. I used the AI4I 2020 dataset: 10,000 synthetic runs, 3.39% failures, five failure modes. From five sensor readings I built 16 model inputs, including power from torque and speed, the temperature gap, and wear times torque, because those are the physics behind the failure modes. I trained logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting on a stratified split and tracked everything in MLflow. Gradient boosting won on F1 with 0.85, AUC 0.96, and was registered. Random forest actually had the higher AUC, 0.98, so the choice depends on the threshold. Around the model, FastAPI serves predictions and questions. A Kafka producer replays rows as a sensor stream, and a consumer keeps a 100 record window and raises alerts on failure rate, torque, and tool wear. The RAG side chunks six maintenance procedures, embeds them into ChromaDB, retrieves four chunks with MMR, and answers with gpt-4o-mini, citing the document. Airflow retrains nightly behind a 0.80 F1 gate. Now the honest part. The data is synthetic, and my features mirror the rules that generated the labels, so the score mostly shows the pipeline works. Reading the code back, the gate doesn't gate, because training registers the model before the branch and the API serves the latest version. The serving path also encodes every product grade the same way, and the stream never calls the model. Next I'd fix those seams with integration tests, which is exactly what my follow up project focused on.

narration.prompt: Give me the full technical story, as you would to a staff engineer.
narration.script: Start with the data, because it explains the numbers. AI4I is synthetic. Four of its five failure modes are deterministic rules. Heat dissipation fails when the temperature gap is under 8.6 kelvin and speed is under 1380 rpm. Power fails outside 3500 to 9000 watts. Overstrain fails when wear times torque passes a limit that depends on the product grade. I engineered exactly those quantities: power as torque times two pi times rpm over sixty, the temperature gap, wear times torque, and power band flags. With five raw readings, the grade, and ten derived features, that's 16 inputs. So a tree ensemble can recover the generator almost directly, which is why the scores are high and why they don't transfer. Training uses one stratified 80 20 split. That leaves about 68 failures in the test set, so a couple of predictions move F1 by a point. Logistic regression with balanced weights got 0.31 F1 but 0.95 AUC. Balancing shifts its probabilities up, so at 0.5 it flags too many runs. Random forest got the best AUC, 0.98, and 0.84 F1. Gradient boosting, with 200 trees at depth 6 and subsampling, got 0.85 F1 and was selected on F1 at the default threshold. I logged five fold cross validated F1 for every model and never reported it, which I'd fix. In maintenance, F1 is the wrong objective anyway. The threshold should come from what a missed failure costs against a false alarm. MLflow logs params, metrics, the model with an input example, and importances. The best run gets registered as failure predictor, and the API loads the latest version at startup. Here is the first seam. The Airflow DAG has a 0.80 F1 branch, but the train task registers the model before that branch runs, and the register task only prints. Since serving reads latest, the gate never protects production. The fix is to register inside the gated task and serve by a champion alias. Second seam: serving calls the same feature function as training, which is good. But it refits a label encoder on a single row, so every grade becomes zero, which meant H in training. That understates overstrain risk for L and M parts. Third: the Kafka consumer computes a rolling failure rate from the ground truth label in each replayed record and never calls the model. On a real line that label arrives later. The RAG side is cleaner. It uses 800 character chunks with 100 overlap, small OpenAI embeddings in ChromaDB, MMR for four chunks out of eight, and a stuff chain with a prompt that requires citations. But nightly re ingestion appends duplicates, and nothing evaluates answers. The Compose file has nine entries, which is seven services if Airflow counts once. The Airflow containers lack the config mount, the MLflow address, and a shared metadata database. The common cause is integration claims without integration tests. My next project, the ZTF pipeline, was designed around closing exactly these gaps, with real data, a tested warehouse, and claims sized to the evidence.

narration.prompt: Explain it to someone who is not an engineer.
narration.script: Factories lose money when machines break without warning. I built a system that looks at a machine's sensor readings, like temperature, speed, and how worn the cutting tool is, and estimates whether it's about to fail. It also watches a live feed of readings and raises an alert when things look off, and it has a chat assistant that answers questions from the maintenance manuals. I tested it on a public practice dataset of 10,000 simulated machine runs, where it caught failures well. Because the data is simulated, the real proof would come from a factory's own machines. Looking back, I also found places where the parts didn't connect the way I'd described, and fixing that shaped my next project.

narration.prompt: Why does logistic regression have such a low F1 with a high AUC?
narration.script: AUC measures ranking over every threshold, and F1 is one threshold, 0.5. I trained logistic regression with balanced class weights, which tells the loss to treat failures as if they were half the data. That pushes failure probabilities up, so at 0.5 it flags lots of normal runs. Recall is high, precision collapses, and F1 follows the weaker one. The ranking is still good, so AUC stays at 0.95. A linear model also can't represent the failure rules without interaction terms, like the heat rule needing both a small temperature gap and low speed. Tuning the threshold on validation data would raise its F1 a lot.

narration.prompt: How would you pick the alert threshold for a real plant?
narration.script: From costs, not from F1. If a missed failure costs a lot more than an inspection, the threshold should sit well below 0.5. For calibrated probabilities, the cost optimal threshold is the false alarm cost divided by the sum of both costs. So I'd first calibrate the model on held out data, since boosted trees aren't calibrated by default. Then I'd get rough costs from maintenance, plot expected cost against the threshold on validation data, and pick the minimum. If the crew can only inspect so many machines a shift, I'd flag the top few by risk instead. And I'd track precision and recall in production once real failure labels come back.

narration.prompt: How would you make the promotion gate real?
narration.script: Right now training registers the model before the gate, and the API serves whatever version is newest. I'd change three things. Train with registration off and pass the run id through XCom. In the gated task, register the model and move a champion alias, and only if it clears the threshold and beats the current champion on the same data. Then the API loads the model by that alias, so a registered but unapproved version never serves. I'd add a test that runs the DAG logic with a model under 0.80 and asserts the alias didn't move. Stages are deprecated in MLflow, so aliases are the right tool.

narration.prompt: What would you change in the streaming layer?
narration.script: Two things. First, the consumer computes a rolling failure rate from the failure label in each replayed record, and on a real line that label arrives after the fact. So I'd score each record with the registered model inside the consumer and alert on predicted risk instead. Second, keys. The producer keys by product grade, which gives three keys with half the traffic on one. I'd key by machine, so each machine's readings stay in order on one partition and consumers can scale out. I'd also keep the window state somewhere that survives a restart, and commit offsets after an alert is published rather than on a timer.

narration.prompt: 0.85 F1 on synthetic data with published rules tells me nothing.
narration.script: About real machines, agreed, and I say the data is synthetic in the first line of my limitations. My features compute the same quantities the label rules use, power, temperature gap, wear times torque, so the model is largely rediscovering the generator. What the number does show is that the pipeline works end to end, from features through MLflow to a served model. If I wanted a claim about prediction, I'd need real plant data, a time based split, and labels from maintenance logs. That's the reason my next project moved to a real public data stream.

narration.prompt: Your write up says a bad batch never reaches production. Your code says otherwise.
narration.script: You're right, and I'd rather say it first. The train task registers the best model before the branch that checks 0.80 F1, the register task only prints, and the API loads the latest version. So a weak model would still become the newest version and get served after a restart. The DAG has the right shape: quality check, train, branch on a metric, conditional promotion, and a downstream refresh with the right trigger rule. The wiring is wrong. The fix is to register and move a champion alias only in the gated task, serve by alias, and test that a weak model can't move it.

cards.q: What problem does ShopFloor AI solve, in one sentence and then technically?
cards.easy: It predicts which machining runs are about to fail from five sensor readings, watches a live stream of readings for warning signs, and lets an operator ask questions about maintenance procedures in plain English.
cards.deep: Three subsystems behind one API. (1) Failure prediction: a binary classifier over the AI4I 2020 milling dataset (10,000 synthetic records, 3.39% failures across five failure modes), with 16 model inputs (5 raw sensors plus 11 engineered), three scikit-learn models compared and tracked in MLflow, and the best by F1 registered. (2) Streaming: a Kafka producer replays the dataset as a sensor stream and a consumer keeps a 100 record rolling window, computes KPIs, and publishes threshold alerts to an alerts topic. (3) RAG: six hand written maintenance SOPs chunked, embedded with OpenAI embeddings into ChromaDB, retrieved with MMR, and answered by gpt-4o-mini through a LangChain RetrievalQA chain. FastAPI serves /predict, /ask, /health; Streamlit is the front end; Airflow schedules a nightly retrain; Docker Compose runs it. The write up frames the engineering around the model as the point, and lists the synthetic data and replayed stream as limitations.

cards.q: What is the AI4I 2020 dataset?
cards.easy: A public, synthetic dataset of 10,000 milling machine runs with five sensor readings, a product quality grade, and whether the machine failed. About 3.4% of runs fail, through five different failure types.
cards.deep: From the UCI page: 10,000 rows, synthetic but modeled on real predictive maintenance data, CC BY 4.0. Columns: UDI, Product ID, Type (L 50%, M 30%, H 20%), air temperature (random walk, std 2 K around 300 K), process temperature (random walk, std 1 K, plus air temperature plus 10 K), rotational speed (from a 2860 W power with noise), torque (normal around 40 Nm, std 10, no negatives), tool wear (H, M, L add 5, 3, 2 minutes per process), Machine failure, and five mode flags TWF, HDF, PWF, OSF, RNF. cards.q: How are the five failure modes generated in AI4I, and why does that matter for your model?
cards.easy: Each failure type comes from a simple written rule: tools fail between 200 and 240 minutes of wear, heat failures need a small temperature gap and low speed, power failures need power outside a band, overstrain needs wear times torque past a limit, and a tiny share fail at random.
cards.deep: Rules per the UCI description: TWF at a tool wear time chosen between 200 and 240 minutes; HDF when process minus air temperature is below 8.6 K and speed below 1380 rpm; PWF when power (torque times angular speed) is below 3500 W or above 9000 W; OSF when tool wear times torque exceeds 11,000 minNm for L, 12,000 for M, 13,000 for H; RNF with 0.1% probability regardless of inputs. Why it matters: four of five modes are deterministic thresholds on simple functions of the inputs, and the engineered features compute exactly those functions (temp_diff, power_W, power_low below 3500, power_high above 9000, wear_torque_product). A tree ensemble can then learn the generating rules almost directly, which explains high scores and also means the score is a measure of rule recovery on a synthetic process rather than of predictive skill on a real machine. RNF is irreducible by construction, and the TWF window is randomized, which together bound how good any model can be.
evidence: repo:shopfloor-ai/src/data/sop_documents.py: threshold (11000 for L, 12000 for M, 13000 for H variants).

cards.q: What are the 16 features?
cards.easy: Five raw sensor readings, the product grade as a number, and ten derived features: temperature gap, power, wear times torque, wear as a share of tool life, torque per rpm, two power band flags, a heat risk flag, and two rescaled temperatures.
cards.deep: From src/ml/features.py: raw air temperature, process temperature, rotational speed, torque, tool wear (5); type_encoded via LabelEncoder (1); temp_diff = process minus air; power_W = torque x (2 pi x rpm / 60); wear_torque_product = tool wear x torque; tool_wear_ratio = wear / 240; torque_per_rpm = torque / (rpm + 1); power_low = power_W < 3500; power_high = power_W > 9000; hdf_risk = temp_diff < 10 and rpm < 1500; air_temp_norm = (air minus 300) / 2; process_temp_norm = (process minus 310) / 1 (10). So '16 features derived from 5 raw readings' means 16 model inputs, 11 of them derived. Three are exact linear rescalings of raw columns (tool_wear_ratio, air_temp_norm, process_temp_norm), which add nothing for trees and add collinearity for logistic regression. hdf_risk uses looser cutoffs (10 K, 1500 rpm) than the dataset's HDF rule (8.6 K, 1380 rpm), while the API's risk factor text uses the exact ones. fillna(0) guards missing values.

cards.q: Derive the power feature and say why the physics features help.
cards.easy: Power is torque times rotational speed in radians per second. Speed in rpm is turned into radians per second by multiplying by 2 pi and dividing by 60.
cards.deep: $P = \tau\,\omega$, $\omega = 2\pi n/60$, so $P[\mathrm{W}] = \tau[\mathrm{Nm}] \cdot 2\pi n[\mathrm{rpm}]/60$. At the dataset's typical 40 Nm and about 1500 rpm, $P \approx 40 \cdot 157 \approx 6283$ W, inside the 3500 to 9000 W band. Heat: $\Delta T = T_{process} - T_{air}$, and HDF needs $\Delta T < 8.6$ K with $n < 1380$. Overstrain: $w \cdot \tau$ against 11,000, 12,000, 13,000 minNm by grade. Why they help: a tree splitting on raw torque and rpm needs many axis aligned splits to approximate a product or a curve like $P = c$, while one split on power_W captures the PWF boundary exactly; a linear model cannot represent $\tau \cdot n$ at all without the product term. The cost is that the features encode the label generating rules of a synthetic process, which inflates scores relative to what the same features would earn on real machines with noisy, unknown failure physics.

cards.q: Explain gradient boosting at textbook depth.
cards.easy: Gradient boosting builds many small decision trees one after another, each trained to fix the mistakes the earlier trees still make, and adds them up with a small weight.
cards.deep:
Model $F_M(x) = F_0(x) + \sum_{m=1}^{M} 
u\, h_m(x)$. For binary log loss $L = -[y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)]$ with $p = \sigma(F)$, the negative gradient at step $m$ is the residual $r_i = y_i - p_i$; a regression tree $h_m$ is fit to the $r_i$, leaf values are set by a Newton step, and the update is scaled by the learning rate $
u$. Here $M = 200$, $
u = 0.1$, max_depth 6 (so trees can model interactions up to depth 6), and subsample 0.8, which fits each tree on a random 80% of rows (stochastic gradient boosting), reducing variance and acting as regularization. Strengths: handles mixed scales without scaling, captures thresholds and interactions such as wear times torque. Failure modes: overfits with deep trees and many rounds without early stopping (none is used here), probabilities are not calibrated by default, and there is no class weighting in this configuration, so the minority class is learned only through the loss.

cards.q: Explain random forest and class_weight balanced.
cards.easy: A random forest trains many deep trees on random samples of the data and random subsets of features, then averages their votes. Balanced class weights make each failure count more during training so the rare class is not ignored.
cards.deep: Each tree is grown on a bootstrap sample with a random feature subset considered at each split, which decorrelates trees so averaging reduces variance: for $B$ trees with pairwise correlation $\rho$ and variance $\sigma^2$, the average's variance is $\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$. Here 200 trees, max_depth 12, min_samples_split 5, n_jobs -1. class_weight balanced sets $w_c = \frac{n}{k\, n_c}$; with 3.39% failures and $k = 2$, a failure weighs about $1/(2 \times 0.0339) \approx 14.7$ and a pass about $0.52$, so failures carry roughly 28 times the weight of passes. Probabilities are mean leaf class fractions, which tend to be pulled toward the middle. Result here: the best AUC (0.9823) but slightly lower F1 (0.8387) than gradient boosting at the 0.5 threshold, which suggests its ranking is better and its 0.5 cutoff is not the best operating point.

cards.q: Why did logistic regression get 0.31 F1 but 0.95 AUC?
cards.easy: It ranks failures above normal runs well, but the default cutoff makes it flag far too many normal runs as failures. Ranking quality and the quality of one yes or no cutoff are different things.
cards.deep: AUC measures ranking across all thresholds; F1 is computed at one threshold, 0.5. With class_weight balanced, the loss treats the two classes as equally frequent, which shifts predicted probabilities upward for the minority class, so at 0.5 the model predicts many positives: recall is high, precision collapses, and F1, the harmonic mean, is dragged toward the low precision. That is Tanay's reading of the pattern; the per model precision and recall were logged to MLflow but are not in the repo's reported table. The linear model also cannot represent the generating rules without help: the HDF rule is a conjunction, the PWF rule is a band (two sided), and the OSF limit depends on grade. Fixes: tune the threshold on validation data, use class weights without the threshold shift, or add interaction terms.

cards.q: Define precision, recall, F1, and AUC-ROC, and say what 0.85 and 0.96 mean here.
cards.easy: Precision is how many flagged failures were real. Recall is how many real failures were caught. F1 balances the two. AUC is the chance the model scores a random real failure above a random normal run.
cards.deep: $P = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}$, $R = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}$, $F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P+R}$, the harmonic mean, so it is dominated by the weaker of the two. $\mathrm{AUC} = \Pr(s(x^+) > s(x^-))$, the area under TPR against FPR over all thresholds. F1 0.8548 at threshold 0.5 on roughly 68 test failures means precision and recall are both around the mid 0.8s or one is higher and the other lower; the split was not reported, which matters because a missed failure and a false alarm cost different amounts. AUC 0.9591 means about 96% of failure and non failure pairs are ordered correctly. At 3.39% prevalence ROC AUC can look strong while precision is weak, since false positive rate is divided by about 1,932 negatives; PR-AUC (average precision) is the better summary for a rare positive class, and it was not computed.

cards.q: What threshold does the system use, and how should it be chosen?
cards.easy: It uses 0.5, the default. In maintenance the threshold should come from costs: if missing a failure costs much more than an extra inspection, you should flag at a much lower probability.
cards.deep: /predict returns failure_prediction = proba >= 0.5 and model selection used F1 at 0.5, so the operating point was never tuned. Decision theory: flag when $p\,c_{FN} > (1-p)\,c_{FP}$, so the cost optimal threshold for calibrated probabilities is $t^* = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}$. As an illustration, not a project number: if an unplanned breakdown costs ten times an inspection, $t^* = 1/11 \approx 0.09$. Two prerequisites: probabilities must be calibrated (gradient boosting and random forest are not by default, so fit Platt or isotonic calibration on held out data), and the threshold must be picked on validation data, not the test set. A capacity constrained alternative is to flag the top k riskiest runs per shift, which is where AUC and precision at k matter more than F1.

cards.q: What do F1 0.85 and AUC 0.96 mean for maintenance cost?
cards.easy: On their own, not much in money. Cost depends on how many real failures are missed and how many false alarms send someone to inspect a healthy machine, and on what each of those costs on a given shop floor.
cards.deep: Expected cost per run at threshold $t$: $C(t) = c_{FN}\cdot FN(t) + c_{FP}\cdot FP(t)$ (plus the cost of acting on true positives, often a planned tool change). F1 weighs FN and FP equally, which is rarely true in maintenance, where a missed failure means unplanned downtime, scrap, or damage while a false alarm is an inspection. So the right reporting is a confusion matrix at the chosen threshold, translated with plant specific costs, plus a curve of cost against threshold. A high AUC says a good threshold exists; it does not say the 0.5 threshold is it. And on AI4I, part of the score comes from features that mirror the generating rules, so any cost estimate here would be an exercise, not a forecast. The SOP bundled with the project sets a failure rate target under 3.5%, which is a process KPI, not a model metric.

cards.q: Random Forest had the higher AUC. Why did you pick Gradient Boosting?
cards.easy: Because the selection rule was F1 at the default threshold, where gradient boosting led 0.8548 to 0.8387. That rule is defensible but not the only one, and with tuned thresholds random forest could win.
cards.deep: Concede: RF's AUC 0.9823 beats GB's 0.9591, meaning RF ranks failures better overall; F1 at 0.5 reflects one operating point, and the gap (0.016 F1) is small relative to the noise on about 68 test positives. Defend: a deployed classifier has to commit to a decision rule, and at the shipped rule GB made the better yes or no calls on the test set. The better procedure: tune each model's threshold on validation data (or by cross validation), compare at cost optimal or fixed recall operating points, report PR-AUC and the CV F1 already logged, and then choose. Tanay would run that before calling either the production model.
cards.say: Fair question. I selected on F1 at the default threshold, where Gradient Boosting edged it out. Random Forest ranked better, so after threshold tuning it might win, and the gap is small for about 68 test failures. Next time I'd tune thresholds on validation data and compare at the operating point I'd actually deploy.

cards.q: How does a model get promoted to serving?
cards.easy: After training, the script registers the best model as a new version in MLflow's registry. The API loads whichever version is newest when it starts. There is no separate approval step or production label.
cards.deep: train_and_evaluate(register_best=True): best_name by F1, then mlflow.search_runs filtered on params.model_type = best_name, ordered by metrics.f1 DESC, max 1, and mlflow.register_model('runs:/<run_id>/model', 'failure-predictor'), which creates a new version (version numbers increment). Serving: FastAPI's lifespan calls mlflow.sklearn.load_model('models:/failure-predictor/latest'), the newest version, once at startup; a newly registered version is only served after an API restart. Two subtleties: search_runs scans every run in the experiment, so it can register an older run of the same model type with a higher F1 than tonight's; and nothing sets a stage or alias. MLflow now deprecates stages in favor of aliases, and the standard pattern is to load models:/failure-predictor@champion and move the alias only after a gate passes, which separates 'registered' from 'deployed'.

cards.easy: Listeners are the addresses the broker tells clients to use. A consumer group shares the work of reading a topic and remembers its place. Delivery is at least once by default: a crash after processing but before the auto commit replays messages, which for a rolling window double counts them.

cards.q: Define RAG, embeddings, a vector store, chunking, and a stuff chain.
cards.easy: RAG means looking up relevant text first and giving it to the language model so it answers from that text. An embedding is a list of numbers that captures meaning. A vector store finds the stored chunks closest in meaning to a question. Chunking cuts documents into pieces small enough to retrieve. A stuff chain pastes all retrieved pieces into one prompt.
cards.deep: Retrieval augmented generation grounds a generator in retrieved evidence, which reduces hallucination on domain facts and lets content change without retraining. text-embedding-3-small maps text to a dense vector; similarity is usually cosine, $\cos(u,v) = \frac{u\cdot v}{\|u\|\|v\|}$. ChromaDB stores vectors with metadata and runs approximate nearest neighbor search. Chunk size trades context per hit against precision: 800 characters with 100 overlap keeps a numbered SOP subsection mostly intact and avoids cutting a threshold sentence in half. The stuff chain is the simplest combine step; map reduce or refine chains exist for when retrieved text exceeds the context window, which four 800 character chunks never do.

cards.q: What is MMR retrieval, and why use it here?
cards.easy: Maximal marginal relevance picks chunks that are relevant to the question but not too similar to chunks already picked, so the four results cover more ground instead of repeating one passage.
cards.deep: Greedy selection from the fetch_k = 8 nearest candidates: $\mathrm{MMR} = \arg\max_{d_i \in C \setminus S}\left[\lambda\, \mathrm{sim}(d_i, q) - (1-\lambda)\max_{d_j \in S} \mathrm{sim}(d_i, d_j)\right]$, repeated until $|S| = k = 4$; LangChain's default $\lambda$ is 0.5 (lambda_mult), which the repo does not override. Why here: the six SOPs overlap heavily (the predictive maintenance protocol, temperature, and power documents all restate the failure thresholds), so plain top k would often return near duplicates of the same threshold list. MMR also partly masks a real bug: re ingesting appends duplicate chunks, and MMR's redundancy penalty keeps exact duplicates from filling all four slots. Tradeoff: with only 8 candidates and a 0.5 weight, a highly relevant second chunk from the same document can be dropped in favor of a less relevant one from another document.

cards.q: What happens to the vector store when the nightly DAG re ingests the SOPs?
cards.easy: It adds a second copy of every chunk each time, because the ingest step never clears the collection or gives chunks fixed ids. After a week of nightly runs the store holds many copies of the same text.
cards.deep: RAGEngine.ingest calls Chroma.from_documents into the existing milling_sops collection with no ids and no delete, so each call appends new vectors with fresh ids. The Airflow refresh_rag task and the /rag/ingest endpoint both call it. Effects: storage and embedding cost grow linearly with runs; top k retrieval would return duplicates, which MMR partly hides; and a changed SOP's old chunks would stay retrievable alongside the new ones, so a superseded threshold could still be quoted. Fix: deterministic ids from a hash of (title, chunk index, content) with upsert, or delete the collection before re ingesting, and record a document version in metadata so answers can cite which revision they used.

cards.q: How would you evaluate the RAG assistant? What exists today?
cards.easy: Nothing measures it today; the tests only check that six documents exist with a title, a category, and enough text. I would write questions with known answers and known source documents, and score both the retrieval and the answers.
cards.deep: Retrieval: a set of question, gold document, gold passage triples (for example 'What power range triggers PWF?' with the Power and Torque SOP), scored by recall at 4 and MRR, comparing similarity search against MMR and chunk sizes. Generation: exact match or a rubric for numeric facts (3500 W, 9000 W, 8.6 K, 1380 rpm), faithfulness (every claim supported by a retrieved chunk), citation accuracy (the cited title is the gold one), and refusal on out of scope questions, which the prompt asks for. Regression: run it in CI on every prompt or chunking change. The SOPs were authored for this project, so a good score shows the plumbing; the write up's own limitation says organization specific documents would improve relevance.
evidence: portfolio: Bundled SOPs. RAG answers depend on the 6 shipped documents
repo:shopfloor-ai/README.md: Runs 15 unit tests covering data loading, feature engineering, streaming logic, and SOP document structure.

cards.q: Six documents. Why ChromaDB, LangChain, and an embedding model at all?
cards.easy: For six documents you could paste everything into the prompt. The vector store is there to learn and show the pattern that matters once there are thousands of documents, and I'd say that directly.
cards.deep: Concede: the six SOPs together are a few thousand words, which fits in gpt-4o-mini's context window; full context stuffing would be simpler, cheaper to operate, and could answer more accurately because nothing is missed by retrieval. Defend: the pattern (chunking, embeddings, metadata for citation, MMR, a retrieval chain behind an API) is what an organization's real document set needs, the write up names the six bundled documents as a limitation, and the retrieval step gives citations per chunk. What Tanay would add before arguing retrieval beats stuffing: the evaluation above, run against a full context baseline.
cards.say: Fair. Six documents fit in the prompt, and stuffing them all in would probably answer just as well. I built the retrieval pattern because that's what a real document set needs, and my write up names the six bundled documents as a limitation. Before claiming retrieval helps, I'd evaluate it against a full context baseline.
evidence: portfolio: Bundled SOPs. RAG answers depend on the 6 shipped documents

cards.q: Describe the FastAPI service.
cards.easy: It loads the model and the chat chain when it starts, then offers endpoints to predict failure from sensor readings, ask a question, re index the documents, and check health.
cards.deep: Lifespan context manager: read config, set the MLflow URI from env, load models:/failure-predictor/latest (a warning, not a crash, if it fails), build the RAG chain (also tolerant). GET /health returns model and rag readiness. POST /predict takes SensorInput, a pydantic model whose fields carry the dataset's column names as aliases with defaults (300 K, 310 K, 1500 rpm, 40 Nm, 100 min, M) and populate_by_name; it builds a one row DataFrame, runs engineer_features, takes predict_proba, and returns failure_prediction (proba >= 0.5), failure_probability rounded to 4 places, and rule based risk_factors: wear above 200, power outside 3500 to 9000 W, HDF when temp gap < 8.6 K and rpm < 1380, torque above 55 Nm. POST /ask returns 503 if the chain is not ready. POST /rag/ingest re embeds. CORS allows all origins. Endpoints are async def but call blocking sklearn and OpenAI code, which blocks the event loop; plain def handlers would run in the threadpool.

cards.q: Is there any train and serve skew in the prediction API?
cards.easy: Yes, one real bug. The product grade is turned into a number by a label encoder that is refit on each request's single row, so at serving time every grade becomes 0, which during training meant grade H.
cards.deep: engineer_features calls LabelEncoder().fit_transform(df['Type']) inside the function. On the 10,000 row training frame the classes sort to H = 0, L = 1, M = 2. In /predict the frame has one row, so the encoder sees one class and maps it to 0, which the model reads as H whatever grade was sent. Because OSF limits differ by grade (11,000 for L, 12,000 for M, 13,000 for H minNm), serving everything as H understates overstrain risk for L and M parts. Sharing one feature function between training and serving was the right instinct; the fix is to make the encoding stateless (a fixed mapping {L: 0, M: 1, H: 2}) or fit the encoder in the training pipeline and log it with the model, plus a test that scores the same row through both paths and compares.
evidence: repo:shopfloor-ai/src/data/sop_documents.py: threshold (11000 for L, 12000 for M, 13000 for H variants).

cards.q: What is the 7 service Docker Compose topology?
cards.easy: Kafka and its coordinator Zookeeper, the MLflow tracking server, the ChromaDB vector database, Airflow, the FastAPI backend, and the Streamlit dashboard. The compose file has nine entries because Airflow is split into a setup step, a web server, and a scheduler.
cards.deep: docker-compose.yml services: zookeeper (cp-zookeeper 7.6.0, 2181); kafka (cp-kafka 7.6.0, 9092 host and 29092 internal, auto topic creation, offsets replication factor 1); mlflow (v2.16.0, 5000, SQLite store, artifacts bind mounted); chromadb (0.5.0, 8000, persisted to ./data/vectordb); airflow-init (db migrate, admin user); airflow-webserver (8080); airflow-scheduler; api (built from the python 3.11 slim Dockerfile, 8001, uvicorn with reload, depends on kafka, mlflow, chromadb); dashboard (same image, 8501, depends on api). Counting Airflow as one gives seven, which matches the write up; the producer and consumer are not containers and run from the host. depends_on orders startup but does not wait for readiness, which is why the API tolerates a missing model or chain at startup.
evidence: portfolio: The three parts run as seven containerized services rather than a notebook.

cards.q: What doesn't match between the write up, the README, and the repo?
cards.easy: A few small things: the MLflow port, the CI workflow, the environment template, and two descriptions of what the pipeline does.
cards.deep: (1) The write up and README list MLflow at :5001, while docker-compose maps 5000:5000, config.yaml uses localhost:5000, and make up prints 5000. (2) The write up and README mention GitHub Actions CI and the README tree shows .github/workflows/ci.yml, but no .github directory is in the repository. (3) make setup copies .env.example, which is not in the repository either. (4) The README says the data quality gate checks value ranges; the DAG does not. (5) The write up says the streaming layer keeps predictions current and the gate keeps a bad batch out of production; the code does neither as written (see the streaming and gate cards). (6) The README tree marks the dataset as gitignored, but there is no .gitignore. None changes a reported number; each is a credibility detail an interviewer who opens the repo could notice, so it is better raised first.
evidence: portfolio: Services come up on these ports: dashboard (:8501), API docs (:8001/docs), MLflow (:5001), Airflow (:8080).

cards.q: What do the 15 tests cover, and what do they miss?
cards.easy: They check the dataset loads with the right shape and columns, the features have no gaps and sensible power values, the streaming alert rules fire, and the six documents are well formed. They do not test training, the API, the registry, the DAG, or the RAG answers.
cards.deep: tests/test_core.py: TestDataDownload (5): 10,000 rows, required columns, every failure mode present, types exactly L, M, H, schema info; TestFeatures (4): shape and at least 10 columns, no NaNs, engineered columns exist, power_W between 0 and 20,000; TestStreaming (4): processor adds rolling fields, FAILURE_RATE_HIGH after five failures, TORQUE_SPIKE at 70 Nm, TOOL_WEAR_HIGH at 220 min; TestSOPs (2): at least 5 documents, each with title, category, and over 200 characters. Data tests download the dataset on first run, so they need network access. Missing and highest value: a serving parity test (the same row through training features and /predict, which would have caught the label encoder bug), a gate test asserting nothing is registered below 0.80, a FastAPI TestClient test of /predict with a stub model, and a cooldown test for alerts.

cards.q: What does the dashboard show?
cards.easy: Four pages: overall KPIs and failure charts from the dataset, a slider form that calls the prediction API, a chat page for the document assistant, and a page of rolling averages labeled as drift monitoring.
cards.deep: Streamlit app reading API_URL from env. KPI page: total units, failure rate, mean torque, mean tool wear; failure mode counts; failure rate by Type; rpm against torque colored by failure; tool wear histogram by failure (Plotly, dark template). Predictor: sliders for the five sensors and a Type select, posts to /predict, shows probability and risk factors. Chat: session state history, posts to /ask, shows sources in an expander, plus quick question buttons. Drift Monitor: 200 row rolling means of torque and tool wear over the static CSV, captioned that upward trends signal data drift.

cards.q: Your drift monitor is a rolling mean of a static CSV. That isn't drift detection.
cards.easy: Agreed. It shows the shape of two sensors over the dataset's row order. It does not compare live data against the training distribution, and tool wear in this dataset rises and resets by design, so an upward trend there is normal.
cards.deep: Concede: the page plots 200 row rolling means of torque and tool wear from data/raw/ai4i2020.csv; no reference window, no statistic, no threshold, and nothing reads the Kafka stream. Tool wear accumulates per tool and resets at replacement, so its rolling mean trending up is the generator, not drift. Real drift detection compares a recent window to the training distribution per feature with PSI or a KS test, watches the predicted failure rate, and once labels arrive, the model's precision and recall. This gap is one of the things Tanay built properly in the follow up ZTF pipeline, which computes PSI on the prediction distribution from a tested monitoring table.
cards.say: Agreed, it isn't. It's a rolling average of the static dataset, and tool wear rising is just how the data was generated. Real drift detection compares recent data to the training distribution with something like PSI. I built that properly in my next project.
evidence: portfolio: I designed this project to close the three gaps I listed as limitations in ShopFloor AI

cards.q: Seven services for 10,000 rows is over engineered.
cards.easy: For the data volume, yes. The services exist because each is a part of a real ML platform I wanted to wire together and learn: tracking and registry, orchestration, streaming, a vector store, an API, and a UI.
cards.deep: Concede: a notebook plus a pickled model would score this dataset just as well, the stream is replayed, and running Kafka, Zookeeper, MLflow, ChromaDB, three Airflow processes, an API, and a dashboard on a laptop costs memory and start up complexity, and several of the integrations show gaps when read closely (the gate, the Airflow config, the streaming label). Defend: the write up says the interesting engineering is everything around the model, and each service maps to a production concern: training and serving separated by a registry, scheduled retraining, a stream for operational KPIs, and retrieval over documents. The honest lesson Tanay took forward: wire fewer pieces and verify each one with a test, which is how the ZTF pipeline was built.
cards.say: For 10,000 rows, yes. I built it to learn how the platform pieces fit: registry, orchestration, streaming, retrieval. Reading it back, a few of the seams don't hold as written, like the promotion gate. The lesson I took into my next project was fewer pieces, each one verified.
evidence: portfolio: The three parts run as seven containerized services rather than a notebook.
portfolio: 10,000 records at a 3.39% failure rate, across five independent failure modes

cards.q: Your write up says a model must clear 0.80 F1 before promotion. Show me where that's enforced.
cards.easy: It isn't enforced as written, and I'd say so before you found it. The training task registers the model before the gate branch, and the API loads the newest version, so the gate only decides whether a print statement runs.
cards.deep: Concede: retrain_dag.py's train task calls train_and_evaluate(register_best=True), which registers; should_register then chooses between a register task that prints and an EmptyOperator; the API loads models:/failure-predictor/latest. So a model under 0.80 would still become the newest version. Defend what is right: the DAG structure (quality check, train, branch on a metric, conditional promotion, downstream refresh with the correct trigger rule) is the right shape, and the gate threshold is pulled from XCom correctly. Fix: register_best=False in train, register and set a champion alias inside the register task, serve models:/failure-predictor@champion, and add a test that a sub threshold run leaves the alias untouched.
cards.say: It's not enforced, and I'd rather tell you than have you find it. Training registers before the branch, and the API loads the latest version, so the gate just decides whether a print runs. The DAG shape is right. The fix is registering only in the gated task and serving by a champion alias.
evidence: portfolio: A newly trained model must clear a 0.80 F1 threshold in the nightly pipeline before it can be promoted, so a bad batch never reaches production.

cards.q: Why classical ML and not a neural network or a time series model?
cards.easy: Because the data is a table of independent rows with 16 features, where tree ensembles are the standard strong baseline, and AI4I has no real time order per machine to model.
cards.deep: Tabular data with a few thousand rows of signal and threshold shaped decision boundaries is where gradient boosted trees reliably match or beat neural networks, train in seconds, and need no feature scaling. AI4I rows are separate processes rather than a per machine sensor history, so sequence models (LSTMs, temporal convolutions) have nothing to exploit; on real equipment with continuous sensor histories, remaining useful life models and sequence features become the right choice. Logistic regression was included as the linear baseline and showed why the interactions matter.
cards.say: It's a table of independent rows, so boosted trees are the strong baseline and they train in seconds. There's no per machine history in AI4I for a sequence model to use. On real equipment with sensor histories, I'd look at remaining useful life models.

cards.q: What went wrong, looking back?
cards.easy: The parts each work on their own, but several connections between them do not do what the write up says: the promotion gate, the streaming predictions, the grade encoding at serving time, and the Airflow container setup.
cards.deep: Reading the code back: (1) the 0.80 gate does not block registration and the API serves latest; (2) the consumer never calls the model and computes its failure rate from ground truth labels; (3) the label encoder refit per request maps every grade to H at serving; (4) the Airflow containers lack configs, the MLflow URI, and a shared metadata database; (5) nightly RAG refresh duplicates every chunk; (6) the CI workflow and .env.example referenced in docs are not in the repo, and the MLflow port is documented as 5001 but mapped to 5000; (7) the drift page is a rolling mean of a static file. The pattern is integration claims without integration tests. That diagnosis is what shaped the next project: the ZTF pipeline lists closing ShopFloor's gaps as its purpose, runs on real data through a real broker, and has a tested warehouse layer.
cards.say: Each piece worked alone, but the seams between them didn't do what I claimed. The promotion gate didn't gate, the stream didn't use the model, and serving encoded every product grade the same way. The common cause was no integration tests, and fixing that was the whole point of my next project.

cards.q: Compare ShopFloor AI with the ZTF pipeline that followed it.
cards.easy: ShopFloor used a synthetic dataset, a replayed stream with no warehouse, and a model with no real baseline. ZTF moved to real public telescope alerts over a real broker, added a tested warehouse layer, and was more careful about what it claimed.
cards.deep: ShopFloor: AI4I synthetic table, Kafka replay of CSV rows as JSON, MLflow registry, nightly Airflow retrain, LangChain RAG, F1 and AUC headline numbers, 15 tests, several integration gaps. ZTF (by the write up, designed to close ShopFloor's three listed limitations): real ZTF Avro alerts replayed through a real Kafka broker, a dbt warehouse with 21 data tests and source freshness, PSI drift monitoring, CI that builds the warehouse, and an explicit statement that its classifier is a placeholder with no accuracy claim. The comparison is a good interview arc: the first project chased a model number on synthetic data; the second treated data contracts and honest claims as the deliverable.

cards.q: What would production need, and what breaks at 10x and 100x?
cards.easy: Real machine data from shop floor systems, predictions on the stream itself, a model gate that actually gates, monitoring that compares live data with training data, and infrastructure that is not one laptop.
cards.deep: Production: MES or SCADA connectors (OPC UA or MQTT into Kafka), per machine keys and event time, labels joined later from maintenance logs, a time based train and test split, calibrated probabilities with a cost based threshold, an alias based registry promotion with champion versus challenger comparison, feature parity tests, PSI or KS drift per feature, and secrets management for the OpenAI key. 10x (100,000 rows or 10 machines streaming): fine for training; the consumer's per message window scan and single process are still fine; MLflow on SQLite starts to strain under concurrent writes, move to Postgres. 100x (millions of events a day across a plant): partition topics by machine and run a consumer group, compute windows with a stream processor (Kafka Streams, Flink, or Spark Structured Streaming) with state stores so a restart does not lose them, serve the model behind a batching model server, move MLflow artifacts to object storage (the write up's planned S3 backed MLflow on ECS), and replace Compose with an orchestrator.
evidence: portfolio: Planned. SHAP explanations in the prediction API, multi model A/B testing in the DAG, WebSocket live dashboard updates, and AWS ECS deployment with S3 backed MLflow storage.

cards.q: What would you do next?
cards.easy: Fix the seams first: make the gate real, serve by alias, fix the grade encoding, score inside the stream. Then add the evaluation the project lacks, and only then the planned features.
cards.deep: Order: (1) gate and registry: register only in the gated task, champion alias, API loads by alias, test it; (2) serving parity: stateless Type mapping and a test running one row through both paths; (3) streaming: score each record with the registered model in the consumer and alert on predicted risk, drop the label based KPI or mark it lagging; (4) evaluation: report cross validated F1 and PR-AUC, tune thresholds on validation data, compare models at a cost based operating point; (5) RAG: idempotent upserts and a small question set with gold sources; (6) infra: mount configs and env into Airflow, Postgres for Airflow and MLflow, restore the CI workflow. Then the write up's planned items: SHAP explanations in /predict, A/B testing of models in the DAG, WebSocket dashboard updates, and ECS with S3 backed MLflow.
evidence: portfolio: Planned. SHAP explanations in the prediction API, multi model A/B testing in the DAG, WebSocket live dashboard updates, and AWS ECS deployment with S3 backed MLflow storage.

cards.q: Define predictive maintenance, OEE, MES, and SCADA.
cards.easy: Predictive maintenance means fixing equipment based on signs it is about to fail rather than on a fixed calendar or after it breaks. OEE is a standard measure of how productive a machine is. MES and SCADA are the factory software systems that collect production and sensor data.
cards.deep: Predictive maintenance sits between reactive (run to failure) and preventive (fixed interval) maintenance: act when a model or rule says failure is near, trading inspection cost against downtime. OEE = Availability x Performance x Quality, and the bundled SOP sets a target of at least 85%. MES (manufacturing execution system) tracks orders, units, and quality on the floor; SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) collects sensor and PLC data from equipment. The write up's limitation says a production deployment would integrate real MES and SCADA feeds instead of the synthetic AI4I table.
evidence: portfolio: Synthetic dataset. AI4I is 10,000 synthetic records

cards.q: Explain ShopFloor AI to a hiring manager for an ML engineering role.
cards.easy: A full ML platform on a public predictive maintenance benchmark: training with tracking and a registry, an API, a stream, retrieval over documents, nightly retraining. Honest about the synthetic data and the seams that need work.
cards.deep: Lead with the platform and the 0.85 F1 with its synthetic caveat in the same sentence, then the registry and DAG, then what reading it back revealed and how that shaped the next project.
cards.say: ShopFloor AI predicts machine failures, streams sensor KPIs through Kafka, and answers maintenance questions with RAG, all as one Docker Compose stack. My gradient boosting model reached 0.85 F1 on the AI4I benchmark, which is synthetic, so I treat that as a pipeline check. Reading it back, I found the promotion gate didn't actually gate. Fixing that kind of integration gap is what my next project was built around.

cards.q: Explain the training to serving path to a staff engineer.
cards.easy: Shared feature function, MLflow registration by best F1, API loads latest at startup. Then name the three defects in that path.
cards.deep: Features in one function used by train and serve; three pipelines logged per run; best F1 registered; API lifespan loads models:/name/latest; defects: registration before the gate, latest instead of an alias, and a label encoder refit per request.
cards.say: Training and serving share one feature function, which was the right call. Training logs three pipelines to MLflow and registers the best by F1, and the API loads the latest version at startup. Three things are wrong in that path. Registration happens before the gate. Serving uses latest instead of an alias. And the grade encoder is refit on each one row request, so every grade becomes the same number.

cards.q: Explain it to a product manager.
cards.easy: Machines fail, and the plant wants warning before they do. The system scores each run for failure risk, raises alerts on a live feed, and lets operators ask how to handle a problem.
cards.deep: Frame the user value: fewer surprise breakdowns, faster answers from procedures. Say the data is a public simulation and the alert threshold should be set from the cost of a missed failure versus an extra inspection.
cards.say: The goal is fewer surprise breakdowns. The system scores each machining run for failure risk, watches a live feed for warning signs, and answers operators' questions from the maintenance procedures. It's built on a public simulated dataset, so the next real step is plant data. And the alert threshold should come from what a missed failure costs compared with an extra inspection.

cards.q: Give the recruiter version in under a minute.
cards.easy: Tanay built a factory AI platform that predicts machine failures, streams sensor data, and answers questions about maintenance documents, using MLflow, Kafka, Airflow, FastAPI, and LangChain.
cards.deep: One number with its caveat, the tool names, and the follow up project.
cards.say: I built a manufacturing AI platform: it predicts machine failures, streams sensor data through Kafka, and has a chat assistant over maintenance documents. My best model hit 0.85 F1 on a public benchmark dataset. It uses MLflow, Airflow, FastAPI, Docker, and LangChain. My next project took the same ideas onto real public data.
